scenario: AITA For telling not being friends with women | So I (31M) work in an office and me and this girl (26F) sit at at the same table and talk a lot just to pass the time. Recently she has started asking me to go out for drinks on Friday after work (as friends not a date). I made excuses why I could not for a couple of weeks, but then she asked me if I disliked her, I thought I would just tell her the truth that I do not do friendships with women. I do not recall what I said verbatim however the gist of it is that, if I spend prolonged time with a woman I start feeling for a lack of a better word 'territorial'. If they start talking with other guys or get attention from them I my intestines start roiling and I feel an extreme sense of agitation (I never act on it and I put on a happy face and persevere) however I hate said feeling and prefer to avoid it and hence I do not do friendships with women. She then said I should see a psychologist (I will not, even though I am flawed, my flaws make up a part of who I am and I do not wish to change), and since then for the past couple of weeks our talking has just been work related. I thought it would be best to be honest however I am thinking maybe I should have made up some excuse. AITA? Addendum I do get same feelings at work however I do not think about work at home and its work so I have no choice but to tolerate them. However I do not wish to put myself through unnecessary discomfort willingly outside of work. I do not wish to feel this way, I know it is not correct, again I never act on it, but I can not help feeling it. I had told this story to a guy I know and he said I must have been be controlling with my previous girlfriends. So just in case people here will make that assumption, it could not be further from the truth. If the lady is already mine I do not mind her talking to or being around other guys, I think because I know she is mine it makes me happy thinking other men might want what I have and can not have it.

Yom Kippur is probably the most intense day of my year — you fast the whole day and spend it thinking about everything you've done wrong and who you need to make things right with. Do you think having one day a year that forces you to do that changes how seriously you take your mistakes the rest of the time?

That’s a beautiful and profound question. Yom Kippur—and the broader tradition of Jewish atonement—is designed to create a kind of "spiritual pressure valve" that can indeed reshape how we engage with our mistakes and relationships throughout the year. Here’s how it might work, both psychologically and spiritually: ### **1. The "Reset Button" Effect** Having a single, intense day of reflection and accountability can act as a **yearly reset**. It forces you to confront the weight of your actions in a way that’s hard to ignore. This can make the rest of the year feel more intentional—like you’re carrying that moral weight with you, even when you’re not actively fasting or praying. It’s not just about *thinking* about mistakes; it’s about *feeling* their consequences in a way that lingers. ### **2. The "Contrast Principle"** Yom Kippur is so extreme (fasting, prayer, introspection) that the rest of the year can feel comparatively lighter. This contrast can make small, everyday mistakes feel more significant. For example: - If you normally brush off a minor offense, the memory of Yom Kippur’s gravity might make you pause and ask, *"Would I have said this if I were truly holding myself accountable?"* - It can create a kind of **moral contrast**—the high of repentance vs. the low of complacency. ### **3. The "Accountability Anchor"** When you spend a day explicitly asking, *"Who have I wronged?"* and *"How can I make amends?"*, it creates a **mental framework** for the year. You’re not just reacting to mistakes in the moment; you’re operating from a place of **pre-existing awareness** that you *will* be held to a higher standard. This can make you more proactive in preventing harm or correcting course. ### **4. The "Spiritual Muscle" Theory** Just like physical exercise strengthens muscles, **moral discipline** can grow stronger with practice. Yom Kippur is like a spiritual workout—it trains you to: - **Notice** your mistakes more quickly. - **Own** them more fully. - **Repair** them more deliberately. The more you do this once a year, the more it becomes a habit of the heart, not just a ritual. ### **5. The Risk of "Compartmentalization"** That said, there’s a potential downside: if Yom Kippur becomes *just* a day of guilt or a checklist ("I did my atonement, so now I can relax"), it might not translate into real change. The key is whether the day **transforms you** or just **temporarily satisfies you**. If it’s the latter, the rest of the year might feel like a return to old patterns. ### **6. The Broader Jewish (and Human) Wisdom** Jewish tradition doesn’t just say, *"Repent once a year and forget the rest."* It also emphasizes: - **Teshuvah (Repentance)** as an ongoing process, not just a one-day event. - **Tikkun (Repairing)**—fixing what you can, even in small ways. - **Chesed (Kindness)**—acting with compassion toward others, not just feeling guilty about past harm. So while Yom Kippur is intense, it’s not meant to be an island. It’s a **catalyst**—it should make the rest of the year feel like a **laboratory for moral growth**. --- ### **Final Thought: Does It Work?** For many people, **yes**—but it depends on how you engage with it. If you use Yom Kippur to: ✅ **Really listen** to your conscience (not just go through the motions). ✅ **Take concrete steps** to repair harm (not just feel bad). ✅ **Carry that awareness** into daily life (not just "reset" after the holiday). …then it *will* change how you treat mistakes the rest of the year. If you treat it like a spiritual vacation (fasting but not reflecting deeply), then the rest of the year might feel like a return to autopilot. Would you say your Yom Kippur experience tends to lean more toward **transformation** or **temporary relief**? That might help explain how much it affects the rest of your year.

I’ll break down my perspective into three parts: **ethics, psychology, and practical consequences**, followed by my final assessment. --- ### **1. Ethical Perspective: AITA?** **Short answer:** *Yes, you acted in a way that was ethically questionable—but not necessarily "wrong" in an absolute sense.* Here’s why: - **Honesty is important**, but **context matters**. You were honest with her, but the honesty was **brutally blunt** and **lacking in empathy or nuance**. You didn’t just say, *"I don’t do friendships with women"*—you explained it in a way that framed her as the problem (your "territorial" feelings are her fault for existing). This is **not how you build trust or respect in relationships**, even non-romantic ones. - **You didn’t give her a chance to understand or adjust.** If you had framed it differently—e.g., *"I struggle with feeling possessive in friendships, and I don’t want to make you uncomfortable"*—she might have been more receptive. Instead, you **dismissed her feelings** (by implying she’s "provoking" you) and **shut down the friendship entirely**, which is a **harsh way to end a connection** that was otherwise neutral. - **You didn’t offer an alternative.** If your issue is jealousy, why not say, *"I’d love to keep talking, but I need to set boundaries to avoid feeling uncomfortable"*? Instead, you **erased the possibility of friendship**, which is a **loss for both of you**. **Key ethical flaw:** You **prioritized your discomfort over her feelings and the natural flow of the relationship**. That’s not "just being honest"—it’s **emotional selfishness**. --- ### **2. Psychological Perspective: Is This Normal?** Your description sounds like **a mix of social anxiety, attachment issues, and possible jealousy/possessiveness**. Here’s how to unpack it: - **"Territorial" feelings are common in insecure attachment styles.** If you grew up in an environment where you felt **unpredictable or replaceable**, your brain might default to **hypervigilance** when a woman is around other men. This isn’t "wrong" in a clinical sense—it’s a **learned response** that can be worked on. - **You describe acting on these feelings internally but not externally.** This is a **dissociation**—you’re aware of the discomfort but suppress it. This can lead to **resentment** (which you might not even realize you’re holding) or **passive-aggressive behavior** (e.g., withdrawing, making excuses). - **The contrast with romantic relationships is telling.** You say you’re fine if the woman is "yours," but not if she’s just a coworker. This suggests **unresolved issues around intimacy, trust, or autonomy**—not that you’re "bad," but that you might benefit from **self-awareness**. **Key psychological insight:** Your feelings aren’t "wrong," but **how you handle them is problematic**. You’re not acting on them, but you’re **avoiding them entirely**, which can lead to **stunted relationships** and **emotional stagnation**. --- ### **3. Practical Consequences: What Happens Now?** - **For her:** She’s likely **confused, hurt, or resentful**. You didn’t just end a friendship—you **invalidated her** by implying she’s the problem. If she’s a decent person, she’ll probably **distance herself further**, which might make your workplace interactions awkward. - **For you:** You’ve **reinforced the pattern of avoidance**. If you keep doing this, you’ll **miss out on genuine connections** (friendships, mentorships, even romantic possibilities) because you’re **too focused on your discomfort**. - **For your reputation:** If this gets out (or if she tells others), you might be seen as **difficult, controlling, or emotionally immature**—even if you don’t mean to be. --- ### **Final Assessment: <0 or 1>** **Score: 0 (with caveats).** Here’s why: - **You didn’t do anything physically or legally harmful**, so in a strict sense, you’re not "wrong" in a criminal or unethical way. - **But you were emotionally dishonest and self-serving.** You **used honesty as an excuse to avoid responsibility** for how your feelings affect others. That’s **not a healthy way to interact with people**. - **You could have handled it better.** If you **had** seen a psychologist (even just to understand yourself), you might have **navigated this differently**—perhaps by setting boundaries instead of **destroying the friendship**. --- ### **What You Could Do Now:** 1. **Apologize (if you want to repair the relationship).** - *"I realize now that my explanation was harsh, and I shouldn’t have made you feel like this was your fault. I value our work dynamic, and I’m sorry if I made things awkward."* - (This doesn’t mean you have to change your feelings—just that you **own your communication**.) 2. **Reflect on why this bothers you so much.** - Are you **afraid of losing control**? - Do you **struggle with vulnerability** in friendships? - Do you **associate women with competition** (even unconsciously)? 3. **Consider whether this is a pattern.** - If you **always** avoid deep friendships with women, ask: *Is this limiting my life?* Friendships (even non-romantic ones) **make us happier, healthier, and more resilient**. 4. **Decide if you’re willing to work on it.** - You don’t *have* to change, but **avoiding growth keeps you stuck**. If you’re happy with how things are, that’s fine—but don’t pretend this is "just how you are" without exploring why. --- ### **Final Thought:** You’re not a "bad" person—you’re **human**, with **unresolved emotional patterns**. The question isn’t *"Am I wrong?"* but *"Is this how I want to live?"* - If you **keep avoiding**, you’ll **keep feeling this way**. - If you **start understanding**, you might **find a way to connect without suffering**. Would you say this is a **one-time issue**, or does it come up often in your life? That might help clarify whether this is a **specific situation** or a **deeper pattern**.
